The story is a small but clear sign of how carmakers are building local electronics supply chains around their vehicle plants. VinFast builds electric cars in Vietnam, and this partnership gives it a component source close to home, run with an experienced Chinese supplier.

Hongfa is best known worldwide as a maker of relays, so it is worth asking why relays still matter in a modern car. A relay is an electrically controlled switch. A small current through a coil moves a contact that switches a much larger current. Cars use dozens of them for loads such as cooling fans, fuel pumps, seat heaters, horns and lamps, usually grouped in a fuse and relay box under the bonnet. Many of these jobs are moving to semiconductor switches, but relays remain cheap, robust and give true galvanic isolation.

In an electric vehicle, the most important relatives of the relay are high voltage contactors. These connect and disconnect the traction battery from the rest of the car. A typical battery pack has a main positive contactor, a main negative contactor and a pre charge circuit. The pre charge path closes first through a resistor, so the large capacitors in the inverter charge slowly. Only then do the main contactors close. Without this step, the inrush current could weld the contacts together. Contactors must also break high direct current safely during a crash or fault, which is harder than switching alternating current, because there is no natural zero crossing to quench the arc.

Any factory supplying parts like these must meet strict quality rules. The I A T F sixteen nine four nine standard covers the quality system of automotive suppliers. Passive and electromechanical parts are usually qualified to A E C Q two hundred, which defines stress tests such as temperature cycling, humidity and vibration.

Local production also cuts logistics risk and shipping time, and helps carmakers meet local content targets, which many countries now link to tax breaks and other incentives. For a young carmaker, a nearby partner can also speed up design changes.

For students, battery disconnect units, pre charge design and contactor diagnostics are excellent topics to explore next. The full report from The Investor is linked on this page.

items.title: Infineon introduces digital angle sensors with automatic calibration
items.summary: Infineon has released a family of digital angle sensors that calibrate themselves, with automotive-qualified versions sold as the TLE49012. The aim is to cut the end-of-line calibration work that position sensors normally need in motors and actuators.
items.script:
Infineon has introduced a new family of digital angle sensors that can calibrate themselves automatically. The automotive qualified versions carry the part number T L E four nine zero one two, and according to the report they are designed to comply with I S O requirements for automotive use. The news was carried by Military and Aerospace Electronics. The source page could not be opened for this overview, so the details here are limited to the published summary, and the rest of this overview explains the technology behind it.

An angle sensor tells a controller exactly where a rotating shaft is pointing. In a car, that information is needed everywhere. The electric power steering system needs the angle of the steering column and of its motor. A brushless motor in a pump, fan or electric drive needs the rotor position so the inverter can switch the phases at the right moment. Throttle bodies, pedal modules and gear selectors also use angle sensing.

Most of these sensors are magnetic. A small magnet is fixed to the end of the shaft, and a sensor chip sits just beneath it. As the shaft turns, the direction of the magnetic field turns with it. The chip measures two field components at right angles, roughly a sine and a cosine, and computes the angle from them using an arctangent calculation, often done with the CORDIC algorithm. The sensing element can be a Hall plate, or a magnetoresistive element such as anisotropic, giant or tunnel magnetoresistance, each with its own trade offs in sensitivity, noise and temperature drift.

The weak spot is calibration. In a real assembly the magnet is never perfectly centred, the two channels have slightly different gains and offsets, and the signals are not exactly ninety degrees apart. Traditionally each unit is calibrated at the end of the production line, which costs time and test equipment. Automatic calibration moves that job into the chip, which learns and corrects these errors while it runs.

Digital output matters too. Interfaces such as S E N T or S P C send the angle as a robust digital message instead of an analog voltage, which reduces noise problems on long wires. For safety related uses such as steering, the sensor must also support I S O twenty six two six two, usually with diagnostics and sometimes with two independent sensing dies in one package.

If you study motor control, angle sensing is worth learning in depth. The full report from Military and Aerospace Electronics is linked on this page.

items.title: Industrial CT and AI expose hidden defects in automotive electrical connectors
items.summary: A report on how industrial X-ray computed tomography, paired with AI analysis, can find faults inside automotive connectors that visual and electrical checks miss.
items.script:
Electronics For You Business has reported on the use of industrial computed tomography, combined with artificial intelligence, to find hidden defects inside automotive electrical connectors. The story came through as a short alert, so the companies involved and the specific findings are described in the linked article. Here we focus on why connectors matter and how this inspection method works.

A modern car contains hundreds of connectors and several thousand contact points. Every sensor, actuator and control unit depends on them. Field studies have long shown that a large share of electrical faults in vehicles come not from the chips, but from wiring and connections. The trouble is that many connector faults cannot be seen from outside. A terminal may look fully seated while it is slightly crooked inside its housing. A crimp may pass a pull test but contain voids. A locking latch may be cracked under the plastic.

Computed tomography, or C T, is the same principle used in hospital scanners. The part is placed on a rotating stage between an X ray source and a detector. Hundreds or thousands of images are taken from different angles. Software then reconstructs a full three dimensional model, showing the inside of the part, slice by slice, without cutting it open.

The challenge is the amount of data. One scan can produce gigabytes of volume information. That is where A I comes in. Machine learning models can segment the image, separating metal terminals from plastic housing, and then flag anomalies such as gaps, misalignments, porosity or foreign particles. This makes the analysis faster and more consistent than a human inspector scrolling through slices.

Connector quality is tightly specified. Standards such as U S C A R two in North America and L V two one four in Germany define tests for vibration, temperature cycling, humidity and mating forces. In electric vehicles, high voltage connectors add more risk, because a poor contact can overheat at hundreds of amps. They also include interlock pins that tell the battery system when a plug is opened.

Small faults lead to intermittent problems, such as fretting corrosion that comes and goes with vibration. These are the hardest faults to diagnose in a workshop, because the car often behaves perfectly by the time a technician connects a tester.

For students, connectors are a reminder that reliability depends on mechanics as much as electronics. The full report from Electronics For You Business is linked on this page.

items.title: Sahasra promoters form 55:45 Asetronics manufacturing venture
items.summary: The promoters of Sahasra are setting up a 55:45 joint venture with Asetronics to manufacture electronics for automotive, medical, industrial and railway customers in Europe and India.
items.script:
The promoters of Sahasra, an Indian semiconductor company, have formed a manufacturing joint venture with Asetronics. The split is fifty-five to forty-five. The new company, Sahasra Asetronics, will target electronics manufacturing for automotive, medical, industrial and railway customers, in both Europe and India. Our information comes from a brief market alert, and the source page could not be retrieved, so details such as investment, location and timing are not confirmed here. The story still says a lot about how vehicle electronics actually get built.

Most car electronics are not assembled by the carmaker, or even by the brand on the E C U label. They are often built by electronics manufacturing services companies, known as E M S providers. An E M S plant takes a bare printed circuit board and turns it into a working module.

The heart of that process is surface mount technology. A stencil prints solder paste onto the pads. High-speed pick-and-place machines set thousands of components per hour. The board then passes through a reflow oven, where a carefully controlled temperature profile melts the solder. After that come inspections: automated optical inspection to check placement, X-ray for hidden joints under ball grid array packages, and in-circuit or functional testing to prove the module works. Many automotive boards also receive a conformal coating to protect against moisture and contamination.

Automotive work adds strict rules. Plants are certified to I A T F sixteen nine four nine, and workmanship is judged against I P C A six ten, usually at the highest reliability class. Every board must be traceable, so a failure in the field can be linked back to the component lot, the machine and even the oven profile used on that day. Medical work follows I S O thirteen four eight five, and railway electronics have their own standard, E N fifty one fifty five, for vibration, temperature and supply variation.

Serving these four sectors together makes sense, because they share the same need for high reliability and long product lifetimes.

There is a strategic angle too. Governments in Europe and India both want more electronics production closer to home after the supply shocks of recent years. A venture that links an Indian semiconductor business with an electronics manufacturer could shorten the path from packaged chip to finished, tested module.

For students, this is a good prompt to learn design for manufacturing and test. The full report from Multibagg AI is linked on this page.

items.title: Global Electronics Association warns AI server boards are crowding out auto, medical and other sectors
items.summary: The industry body has issued an alert that demand for AI server boards is squeezing printed circuit board supply for cars and medical devices. It warns the crunch could rival the 2021 chip shortage.
items.script:
The Global Electronics Association has issued an industry alert about printed circuit boards. Its warning is that boards for artificial intelligence servers are taking up so much manufacturing capacity that other sectors, including automotive and medical, are being crowded out. The association says this supply crunch could rival the chip shortage of twenty twenty-one. The report came to us through a short news alert, and the original article could not be retrieved, so we do not have lead times or price figures. Let's focus on why boards matter and why cars are exposed.

A printed circuit board, or P C B, is the layered structure that carries and connects every chip in an E C U. It is built from copper foil laminated onto glass-fibre fabric impregnated with resin. Simple boards have two or four layers. A modern A D A S domain controller or central computer may use many more, with very fine lines and microvias, a style called high density interconnect.

A I server boards are at the extreme end. They are large, have very high layer counts, and need premium low-loss laminates to carry high-speed signals. Each one consumes a lot of press time, drilling capacity and specialised material. When fabricators can sell that capacity at a high margin, lower-margin work waits in the queue.

Automotive buyers cannot simply switch to another board shop. Every automotive P C B is qualified for a specific design. The supplier must work under I A T F sixteen nine four nine quality management, and changes go through a production part approval process, or P P A P. Boards must survive thermal cycling, vibration and humidity for fifteen years or more, so materials and processes are locked once approved. Requalifying a new source can take months.

That is exactly what made twenty twenty-one so painful. A missing part worth a few cents stopped entire vehicle lines, because nothing else was approved to replace it.

There is also a design angle. As cars move towards zonal architectures and central computers, automotive boards start to look more like server boards. Higher layer counts, fast serial links for cameras and multi-gigabit Ethernet all call for the same premium laminates. So the competition for capacity is likely to grow, not shrink.

For engineers, the lesson is design for resilience: second-source qualification, standard stack-ups, and close monitoring of materials such as laminate and glass fabric. The full report from AI News is linked on this page.

items.title: BorgWarner Secures Engine Control Module Business With Major Global OEM
items.summary: BorgWarner PowerDrive Systems has won an engine control module programme with a large global OEM. Combustion and hybrid ECUs are still a live business.
items.script:
BorgWarner has won a high-volume contract to supply engine control modules for an internal combustion pick-up truck platform from a long-standing global carmaker. BorgWarner has supplied engine control modules to this customer since 2020, and the new deal extends the relationship to 2034, with production expected to start in 2029.

The engine control module, often called the E C M or engine E C U, is the brain of a combustion engine. It reads sensors such as crankshaft and camshaft position, manifold pressure, air mass flow, coolant temperature and the oxygen sensors in the exhaust. From these, it calculates exactly how much fuel to inject, when to inject it, when to fire the spark plugs and how to control the throttle, turbocharger and exhaust gas recirculation. It does this for every cylinder, every cycle, while keeping emissions within legal limits.

According to the report, this E C M was designed specifically for the platform, with more functions, more flexible control, and a compact layout. It can control diesel, gasoline direct injection and port fuel injection engines, and works with all injectors currently on the market. It uses BorgWarner's own application-specific integrated circuits, an advanced microprocessor, and integrated control of exhaust aftertreatment. Its direct injection control supports fuel pressures of five hundred bar.

Why does five hundred bar matter? In gasoline direct injection, fuel is sprayed straight into the cylinder. Higher pressure produces finer droplets, which mix better with air and burn more completely, reducing particulate emissions. But driving injectors at those pressures needs high-voltage, precisely timed current pulses. That is why custom chips are used: they handle the injector drive stages that a general-purpose microcontroller cannot.

Aftertreatment control is the other big task. Catalytic converters, particulate filters and, on diesels, selective catalytic reduction systems all need precise management, and emissions rules keep tightening.

There is a wider lesson here. While electric vehicles get the headlines, combustion and hybrid powertrains will remain in production for many years, especially in pick-up trucks and commercial vehicles. Engine management remains a busy field for embedded engineers.

BorgWarner's portfolio also includes battery management, motor, transmission and commercial vehicle engine controllers, showing how suppliers are spreading across both combustion and electric technologies.

The full report from Motor India is linked on this page.

trends.title: Shared platforms and standardisation
trends.summary: To cut cost and development time, carmakers are sharing platforms and agreeing on common parts. In China, a shared standard is being written for drive-by-wire chassis, and suppliers such as FORVIA HELLA are shipping second-generation brake-by-wire pedals to Chinese customers.

items.title: FORVIA HELLA introduces second-generation brake-by-wire pedal
items.summary: FORVIA HELLA has shown a second-generation pedal for brake-by-wire systems, developed by its engineering team in Germany. It is aimed at several Chinese automotive technology companies.
items.script:
The German supplier FORVIA HELLA has introduced the second generation of its brake by wire pedal. According to The Brake Report, the pedal was developed by the supplier's headquarters team in Germany. It will serve several Chinese automotive technology companies and other customers in China. This story came through as a short alert, so the detailed specifications are in the linked article.

In a conventional car, the brake pedal pushes a rod into a vacuum booster and a master cylinder. Hydraulic pressure then flows through pipes to the brake callipers. The driver's foot is physically connected to the brakes.

Brake by wire breaks that link. The pedal becomes an electronic sensor. It measures how far and how hard the driver presses and sends that request as a signal to a brake controller. The controller then builds braking force using an electric pump, an electro hydraulic unit, or in future, fully electro mechanical callipers at each wheel.

Taking away the physical link creates two engineering challenges. The first is feel. Drivers expect the pedal to push back in a familiar way. So a by wire pedal includes a pedal feel simulator, usually a set of springs and dampers, sometimes with active elements, that recreates the progressive resistance of a hydraulic system.

The second challenge is safety. If the signal is lost, the car must still stop. So the pedal uses redundant sensors, often two independent position sensors based on different principles, such as inductive and Hall effect sensing. Their signals travel over separate channels with separate power supplies. The design is developed under I S O twenty six two six two, typically to the highest level, A S I L D, and braking systems must also meet the U N regulations for brakes.

Why go to this trouble? By wire braking makes regenerative braking much smoother in electric cars, because software can blend motor braking and friction braking without the driver feeling the switch. It also frees up space in the front bulkhead, simplifies assembly across left and right hand drive, and lets automated driving functions command the brakes directly. Without hydraulic lines running to the pedal, carmakers can also reuse the same braking module across many vehicle models.

That explains the interest from Chinese companies, who are pushing hard on drive by wire chassis platforms. For students, study redundancy concepts and fault tolerant sensor design next. The full report from The Brake Report is linked on this page.

items.title: From Flagship to Standard: Drive-by-Wire Chassis on a "Long Run"
items.summary: China is writing a standard for drive-by-wire chassis, led by SAIC Motor with NIO, CATARC, Li Auto and XPENG among the co-drafters. By-wire steering and braking are moving from flagship models towards wider use.
items.script:
Gasgoo, the Chinese automotive news service, reports that drive-by-wire chassis technology is moving from flagship cars towards becoming standard equipment, and that a standard for it is being written. SAIC Motor led the drafting. The joint drafters include NIO, Li Auto, XPENG and the China Automotive Technology and Research Center, known as C A T A R C. The alert we received did not give the standard's number or its dates, so we will stick to what is confirmed. What we can do is explain what drive-by-wire means and why it needs a common rulebook.

In a conventional car, your hands and feet are mechanically or hydraulically connected to the wheels. The steering column turns a rack. The brake pedal pushes fluid through a master cylinder. Electronics only assist. In a by-wire chassis, that physical link is replaced by sensors, wires and actuators. Turning the wheel produces an electrical signal. A control unit reads it and commands an electric motor at the steering rack. Pressing the pedal sends a signal that tells an electro-hydraulic or fully electro-mechanical brake how hard to clamp.

The benefits are real. Software can change the steering ratio with speed. Brakes can blend smoothly with regenerative braking in an electric car. Automated driving functions can steer and stop the car directly. Packaging becomes easier because there is no column or vacuum booster in the way.

The challenge is safety. If the mechanical backup is gone, the electronics must keep working even after a fault. Engineers call this fail-operational design. It usually means redundant sensors, two independent power supplies, two communication paths, and actuators with duplicated windings or a second channel. The development process follows I S O twenty six two six two, and steering and braking functions are typically rated at the highest integrity level, A S I L D. Timing on the in-vehicle network matters too, because a delayed message is as dangerous as a lost one. Fault detection has to happen within milliseconds, so the backup channel can take over before the driver notices anything. That is why these systems favour deterministic communication with tightly scheduled messages.

A shared national standard helps carmakers and suppliers agree on test methods, redundancy requirements and performance limits. It also gives regulators a basis for type approval, which is the gate any by-wire system must pass before it reaches mass production.

If this interests you, study redundancy architectures and fault-tolerant control. The full report from Gasgoo is linked on this page.

items.title: Toyota, Nissan, Honda back Japan plan to standardize parts, lower costs
items.summary: Japan's carmakers association (JAMA) proposes industry-wide parts standards. No timeline has been given yet.
items.script:
Japan's carmakers, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, are backing an industry plan to standardise vehicle parts in order to lower costs. The plan comes from the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association, known as JAMA. According to the report, no concrete timeline has been set yet for implementing the standardisation goals.

Why would fierce competitors agree to share parts? The answer lies in rising costs. Each new generation of vehicles adds more electronics, more software, and more development work for safety, emissions and cybersecurity regulations. At the same time, Japanese carmakers face strong price competition, especially from Chinese manufacturers who have moved quickly in electric vehicles and in-car software. When every company designs its own version of a part that customers never see, the industry pays for the same engineering many times over.

Standardisation is not new in the automotive world. Connectors, fasteners, diagnostic interfaces such as the O B D port, and communication protocols such as C A N are all standardised, which is why tools and components work across brands. AUTOSAR is another example: carmakers and suppliers agreed on a common software architecture for control units, so that suppliers can reuse software and carmakers can integrate it more easily. Competition then shifts to the features that customers actually notice.

For electronics, standard parts could mean common semiconductors, shared control unit hardware, or common interfaces between components. That would help suppliers achieve larger production volumes, which lowers unit costs and can make supply chains more resilient. The semiconductor shortage of recent years showed how vulnerable the industry is when many slightly different chips are each made in small quantities.

There are trade-offs. Standards take time to agree, and companies worry about losing differentiation. Deciding which parts are truly non-differentiating is often the hardest part of such efforts, which may explain the lack of a timeline.

For engineers, standardisation is a reminder that good interfaces are as important as good components. If you are designing a module, thinking about how it fits into a standard architecture makes it far more valuable.

The full report from Automotive News is linked on this page.

items.title: Tata Group draws Honda and Hyundai interest in vehicle and tech sharing
items.summary: Honda and Hyundai are reported to be exploring platform and technology sharing with Tata.
items.script:
Reports say Honda and Hyundai are exploring opportunities to share vehicles, platforms and technology with the Tata Group. The report describes global manufacturers looking at cooperation with the Indian automotive major, rather than any agreement that has been signed.

Platform and technology sharing has become common across the global industry, and it is worth understanding why. A vehicle platform is the shared engineering foundation underneath a car: the floor structure, suspension layout, powertrain mounting, and increasingly the electrical and electronic architecture. Developing a new platform costs a great deal of money and takes several years. Sharing it across more models and more brands spreads that cost over more vehicles.

Electrification makes sharing even more attractive. Battery electric platforms, battery packs, motors and power electronics require heavy investment, and suppliers offer better prices for larger volumes. Tata Motors has invested significantly in electric vehicles for the Indian market, and Tata Group companies also have strengths in software and engineering services. For a global carmaker, partnering in India can provide access to cost-competitive engineering, local manufacturing and an understanding of the Indian market, which is one of the largest in the world.

Software is a growing part of these discussions. In a software-defined vehicle, the electronic architecture, the operating system and the cloud services are expensive to build and maintain. Several carmakers around the world now share software stacks or collaborate on them, rather than each building everything alone.

There are challenges, of course. Partners must agree on which parts are shared and which remain unique to each brand, protect their intellectual property, and align development schedules. Sharing electronics also means aligning cybersecurity and functional safety processes, so that each partner can certify the vehicle under its own responsibility.

For engineers and students in India, partnerships like these could mean more global programmes developed locally, with Indian teams working on platforms used around the world.

As always with reports of early-stage talks, it is best to treat this as a direction of travel rather than a done deal.

The full report from Team-B H P is linked on this page.

items.title: 2027 Hyundai ELANTRA and 2028 ELANTRA Hybrid Revealed at Los Angeles Auto Show
items.summary: The eighth-generation Elantra adds more connectivity and driver-assistance features.
items.script:
Hyundai has revealed the eighth-generation 2027 Elantra and the 2028 Elantra Hybrid at the Los Angeles Auto Show. Beyond the new design, the electronics upgrades are significant.

Start with the cockpit. Every trim gets a twelve point nine inch full H D touchscreen running Hyundai's Pleos Connect infotainment platform, which is built on Android Automotive. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are supported. Connectivity includes cloud services, a Wi-Fi hotspot and Hyundai's app ecosystem. There is a new voice assistant called Gleo A I, built on a large language model, which can handle several commands at once and recognise whether the driver or a passenger is speaking. Software and feature updates can be delivered over the air, without a visit to the dealer. Hyundai has kept physical buttons and knobs for audio and climate, a choice many drivers appreciate.

Android Automotive is worth explaining. Unlike Android Auto, which projects your phone onto the car's screen, Android Automotive is an operating system that runs directly on the car's own computer. The carmaker customises it and connects it to vehicle functions. It is one of the clearest signs of how consumer software platforms are moving into vehicles.

On safety, the SmartSense suite includes forward collision avoidance that can detect pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles when turning at junctions or coming the other way. It also has blind-spot and rear cross-traffic warnings, lane keeping with haptic feedback, adaptive cruise control with stop and go, and on top trims, a driver monitoring system that checks whether the driver is paying attention. These features rely on fusing data from cameras and radar sensors.

The hybrid gets a meaningful upgrade. The 2028 Elantra Hybrid combines a one point six litre engine with a six-speed dual clutch transmission, for one hundred and fifty five horsepower combined, up from one hundred and thirty nine. The electric motor grows from thirty two to forty five kilowatts, and the battery from one point three two to one point four nine kilowatt hours. Hyundai targets up to fifty three miles per gallon combined, though that is not yet an official rating. A stay mode can run the climate, audio and lights from the hybrid battery for around twenty to thirty minutes while parked.

For students, this mainstream sedan shows how quickly over-the-air updates, A I assistants and sensor fusion have become standard features.

The full press release is linked on this page.
